How long before an occupant can claim the land?

Ten years. A Nebraska occupant gains nothing from time unless every element of adverse possession is met for that whole period. The period comes from 25-202, which sets a ten-year limit on actions to recover title or possession of land.

The Nebraska Supreme Court spelled out what the occupant must show in Rentschler v. Walnofer (1979): possession that is actual, continuous, exclusive and notorious, hostile to the record owner, and held under a claim of ownership, for the full ten years. The court added that the land must be used for a purpose it is suited for. The claimant carries the burden and must prove the case by a preponderance of the evidence.

There is no shorter clock for squatters. Moving into a vacant house for a few weeks gives no title. What a short-term intruder can do is create a possession problem the owner then has to resolve through the courts or the police.

Public land follows other rules. Section 25-202(1) says no limitation period runs against a county, city, town, village, school or other listed public body trying to recover roads, streets, alleys, public grounds and town lots.

Occupation that does not count

Several common situations fail the test because the occupier never held the property against the owner's rights. Nebraska decisions draw these lines.

SituationHow Nebraska courts treat it
Living there with the owner's permissionPermissive possession cannot ripen into adverse possession until the change of position is brought home to the owner (Imperial Service Corp. v. Phipps, 1980)
A tenant who stays after the leaseA tenant cannot hold adversely until surrendering possession or giving the landlord unequivocal notice that the lease no longer governs (Kennedy v. Gottschalk, 1941)
A parent and child sharing a propertyPossession between parent and child is deemed permissive (Chase v. Lavelle, 1921)
A co-owner in possessionNotice of a claim to the entire estate must be brought home to the other co-owners plainly and unequivocally (Gramann v. Beatty, 1938)
A claim like a life estateNot a claim of ownership (Lewis v. Poduska, 1992)
An occupant who disclaims title earlyDisclaiming before the period runs bars the claim (Weisel v. Hobbs, 1940)

So a house that a relative or former renter has lingered in for years is not automatically lost. It also explains why owners should put permission in writing and react when a stay turns hostile.

Fences and boundary mistakes

Boundary disputes are where adverse possession is most likely to touch an ordinary homeowner. Several Nebraska decisions deal with fences.

  • In Ohme v. Thomas (1938), parties who treated a fence as the boundary for the full ten years, without interruption, gained title to land that had been wrongly enclosed.
  • In Conkey v. Anderson Farms (1980), the court reasoned the same way where a fence was built as a boundary even though it was not the true line.
  • Weiss v. Meyer (1981) held that adverse possession rests on the occupant's intent as shown by acts, and that the intent can be mistaken. A claimant who occupies up to the wrong line, believing it is the true one, can satisfy the test.

If a neighbor's garage, driveway or fence has sat over the line for a decade, that can surface in a survey or title review just as you try to close. A boundary fix or a recorded agreement is far easier to finish before an offer than during one.

Removing someone with no right to be there

The civil route is a forcible entry and detainer action, and it starts with a written notice to leave. 25-21,220 lists who can be sued this way. That includes tenants holding over and, in subsection (5), a settler or occupier of land without color of title when the complainant has the right of possession.

Before filing, 25-21,221 requires the owner to notify the adverse party to leave. The notice must be served at least three days before the action begins, by leaving a written copy with that person or at the usual place of abode. If the person cannot be found in the county, the notice may be left at or posted on the premises. The Court of Appeals called this three-day notice necessary to obtain an order of restitution in I. P. Homeowners v. Morrow (2003).

The remedy has limits. In Woodsonia Hwy 281 v. American Multi-Cinema (2025), the Nebraska Supreme Court held that a forcible entry and detainer case must be dismissed when the right to possession depends on resolving the defendant's own right in the property. A genuine title dispute belongs in a different action, such as one to quiet title, which is also subject to the ten-year statute under Olsen v. Olsen (2003).

When an unwanted occupant becomes a criminal trespasser

Entering or secretly remaining in a building while knowing you have no license or privilege to be there is first degree criminal trespass, a Class I misdemeanor under 28-520. Second degree criminal trespass covers other places where notice against trespass has been given.

Under 28-521, notice can be given three ways: by telling the person directly, by posting signs in a way likely to catch the intruder's attention, or by fencing or enclosing the land to exclude intruders. Second degree trespass is a Class III misdemeanor. It rises to a Class II misdemeanor if the person defies an order to leave that the owner or an authorized person gives personally.

Someone who walked in uninvited stands differently from a former tenant or family member who once had permission. For the second kind, a written notice to leave and a copy of your deed give you a record of the order the statute refers to.

Protecting a vacant house

The aim is to keep the ten-year clock from ever starting, and to leave a paper trail if someone tests it. A few habits follow from the rules above.

  • Inspect the property on a regular schedule and note the dates. The occupation must be actual, notorious and continuous to count against you.
  • Put any permission to stay in writing, including who may live there and until when.
  • Post notices and keep fences and locks in repair, which lines up with the notice methods in 28-521.
  • Serve the three-day written notice early if someone is staying without consent.
  • Record your own deed. Hadley v. Platte Valley Cattle Co. (1943) held that a fee simple holder under an unrecorded deed does not forfeit title by failing to assert it, but a recorded deed is easier for everyone to see.
  • Do not wait years. The death of the party against whom the statute is running does not stop it, so it continues against heirs (McNeill v. Schumaker, 1913).

That last point matters for inherited houses that sit empty while family members decide what to do.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nebraska houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with an occupant or a possession dispute

An occupied house is harder to sell on the open market, because a buyer is charged with notice of the rights of anyone in actual possession. Grand Island Hotel Corp. v. Second Island Development Co. (1974), cited under 76-238, applies that rule to a tenant in actual possession.

So unresolved occupants and boundary claims tend to come up in the buyer's title review. We buy Nebraska houses as-is, including some with tenants, holdovers or messy ownership history, and we can talk through what a sale would look like. We are not lawyers, so if someone claims ownership of your property, speak with a Nebraska attorney first.

Frequently asked questions

Do squatters have rights in Nebraska?

Only if they meet adverse possession for ten full years under 25-202 and the cases applying it. The occupant must show actual, continuous, exclusive, notorious and hostile possession under a claim of ownership. Time spent there with the owner's permission generally does not count.

How long is the adverse possession period in Nebraska?

Ten years. Section 25-202 limits actions to recover title or possession of land to ten years after the cause of action accrues, and Nebraska courts use the same period for adverse possession.

What notice do I give a squatter in Nebraska before filing for eviction?

A written notice to leave, served at least three days before the action begins under 25-21,221. It can be handed to the person, left at the usual place of abode, or posted at the premises if the person cannot be found in the county.

Is it a crime to stay in someone's house in Nebraska without permission?

It can be. Entering or secretly remaining in a building knowing you have no license or privilege to be there is first degree criminal trespass under 28-520, a Class I misdemeanor. Defying a personal order to leave other property raises second degree trespass to a Class II misdemeanor under 28-521.

Can a former tenant claim my Nebraska house by staying after the lease ends?

Not by simply staying. Under Kennedy v. Gottschalk, a tenant cannot hold adversely to the landlord until surrendering possession or giving unequivocal notice that the lease no longer governs. Holdover tenants can also be removed through forcible entry and detainer under 25-21,220.

Nebraska Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Selling a Nebraska House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Nebraska?

The law behind Nebraska rentals

Nebraska's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act governs residential rentals. It begins at section 76-1401 of Chapter 76 and walks through the life of a tenancy: the rental agreement, deposits, repairs, entry, termination, and the lawsuit to get possession back.

If you own a rental and may sell, these sections matter most. Section 76-1416 covers security deposits and prepaid rent. Section 76-1417 requires disclosure of the manager and of the owner or owner's agent. Section 76-1419 makes the landlord keep the premises fit, and 76-1425 deals with landlord noncompliance. Section 76-1431 covers tenant noncompliance and failure to pay rent, 76-1434 bars landlord liens and distraint, and 76-1439 prohibits retaliation. Sections 76-1440 to 76-1447 run the action for possession from complaint to appeal.

Owners often ask whether listing a house ends a lease. These sections do not make a listing end a lease. Read the lease, and see an attorney before assuming a sale changes what a tenant is entitled to.

Deposits and a sale

Section 76-1416(5) binds the person who holds the landlord's interest at the end of the tenancy to the deposit rules. So at closing, the seller and buyer should write down how the deposit passes over, and the buyer should know the exact amount.

The deposit rules are specific.

  • Prepaid rent and security go first to unpaid rent and to damage from the tenant's breach. Anything left goes back with a written itemization, and the deadline is fourteen days after the tenancy ends.
  • With no forwarding address, the landlord sends the balance and itemization by first-class mail to the last-known address.
  • Money that comes back undeliverable, or stays unclaimed for one year, is treated as abandoned property reported to the State Treasurer.
  • Missing that deadline can cost the landlord the deposit, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A willful failure not made in good faith adds liquidated damages: one month's rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less.

A cash buyer who inherits tenants will typically request the lease, the deposit figure and the payment ledger. Pulling them together early shortens the closing.

Telling the tenant who owns and manages the home

Under section 76-1417, the landlord or the person who signs for the landlord must hand the tenant two names and addresses in writing, no later than the start of the tenancy. The first is whoever is authorized to manage the premises. The second is an owner, or someone acting for the owner, who accepts service of process and gets notices and demands.

A change of owner can send rent and notices to the wrong place. The statute is written for the start of a tenancy and says nothing of handovers, yet seller and buyer should still put the new contact details in writing for the tenant, so rent and repair requests land where they should.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nebraska house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Nonpayment and lease breaches

Section 76-1431 sets a short clock for unpaid rent and a longer one for other breaches. When rent is late, the landlord gives written notice of the nonpayment and of an intent to terminate. Seven calendar days without payment lets the landlord end the agreement.

A material breach, or one touching health and safety, calls for a written notice that names the acts or omissions. The agreement ends no sooner than thirty days after the tenant receives it, unless the tenant cures within fourteen days. Should substantially the same breach recur inside six months, fourteen days' written notice is enough to end it.

SituationWritten notice period
Rent unpaidSeven calendar days to pay
Material breach, first timeFourteen days to remedy; termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt
Same breach repeats within six monthsAt least fourteen days

Court comes after these notices. Section 25-21,221 also calls for notice to the adverse party three days before a forcible entry and detainer action starts. Tenants have remedies for unlawful ouster and exclusion under section 76-1430, which makes any shortcut around the courts a gamble.

When the landlord fails to keep the home livable

Tenants get a matching tool in section 76-1425. If the landlord materially fails the lease, or neglects the section 76-1419 repair duty in a way that hurts health and safety, the tenant can send a written list of the problems. Fourteen days without a fix ends the agreement on a date at least thirty days after the landlord gets the notice. A recurrence inside six months shortens that to at least fourteen days.

Put off repairs and you may face a tenant's claim just as a buyer's inspector arrives. Keep a written repair history, since it protects both sides. The act has separate sections on failure to supply heat, water and essential services (76-1427), fire or casualty damage (76-1429), and tenant remedies for unlawful ouster or diminished service (76-1430).

Retaliation and seizing a tenant's belongings

Neither is allowed, though limits apply. Section 76-1439 forbids a landlord from answering a code complaint, or tenants' union activity, with a rent hike, reduced services, or a possession suit or threat of one. The complaint must go to a government agency that enforces housing or building codes and concern a health or safety violation. The retaliated-against tenant gets section 76-1430 remedies and a defense to eviction. Reasonable rent increases and service changes are still permitted.

Section 76-1434 adds that a landlord's lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods cannot be enforced, and that distraint for rent is abolished. An owner preparing a rental for sale should never hold a tenant's property as leverage for unpaid rent.

The act also has special rules for tenants who are victims of domestic violence, including release from the rental agreement and lock changes (sections 76-1431.01 to 76-1431.04). Those rules stand apart from any sale.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nebraska houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How a court eviction works

The act sets its own court procedure for recovering possession. It runs from the action for possession in section 76-1440 through the complaint, summons, trial and writ of restitution, to appeal in section 76-1447. The Judicial Branch describes forcible entry and detainer as a proceeding to restore possession of land to a person who has been wrongfully deprived of it.

Owners who hold rentals through a company should note one rule. Outside Small Claims Court, a corporation or LLC landlord needs an attorney and cannot appear for itself.

With a case already open, speak to the attorney on it before signing a purchase agreement, and have the contract state whether the buyer takes the house occupied.

Preparing to sell with a tenant in place

A rental can sell with the tenant still inside, and paperwork in good order makes it easier. Try this list.

  • Pull the signed lease, any addenda, and the rent ledger.
  • Note the deposit, any pet deposit, and where the funds sit.
  • Make sure no notice of nonpayment or breach is half-finished, because the seven-day and thirty-day clocks run from written notice.
  • List open repair requests and complaints to a code office, since the retaliation rules apply.
  • At closing, hand the tenant written contact details for the new owner and manager.

A tenant behind on rent or a house needing work need not stop you, since an as-is buyer takes the property in its current condition. Cash Home Buyers makes cash offers on Nebraska houses like that. Nothing on this page is legal advice.

Frequently asked questions

How much can a Nebraska landlord charge for a pet deposit?

A pet deposit may be up to one-fourth of one month's periodic rent (section 76-1416). That sits beside a security deposit capped at one month's rent. Housing agencies under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act are not subject to the cap.

How long does a landlord have to give notice for unpaid rent?

Seven calendar days, counted from written notice of nonpayment and of the intent to terminate. Section 76-1431 then lets the landlord terminate if rent is still unpaid.

Who gets the deposit if the landlord sells?

Possibly the buyer. Deposit duties fall on whoever holds the landlord's interest at the end of the tenancy, so put the handling of the deposit in writing at closing.

Can a tenant be evicted for complaining to the city about conditions?

Not for that reason. Section 76-1439 bars retaliation, a possession suit or threat included, over a health or safety complaint to a code agency, although reasonable rent increases stay allowed.

Can an LLC landlord file an eviction case without a lawyer?

No. Except in Small Claims Court, a corporation or LLC landlord must be represented by an attorney.

title: Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Nebraska
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Nebraska House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Nebraska?
We buy Nebraska houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Notice periods by reason

The wait before a Nebraska landlord can go to court varies with the reason. Late rent carries a 7-day notice, a lease violation carries 14 or 30 days, dangerous conduct carries 5 days, and a month-to-month arrangement needs 30 days. All of it must be on paper.

ReasonWritten noticeCan the tenant fix it?
Rent not paid (76-1431(2))7 calendar daysYes, by paying within the 7 days
Material lease breach (76-1431(1))Ends no less than 30 days after receipt if not remedied in 14 daysYes, within 14 days
Same breach again within 6 months (76-1431(1))At least 14 daysNo cure period
Violent crime, illegal drug sales, threats to safety (76-1431(4))5 daysNo right to cure
Month-to-month, no cause (76-1437(2))30 days before the rental dateNot applicable
Week-to-week, no cause (76-1437(1))7 days before the end dateNot applicable

The notice just opens the process. Getting the tenant out still takes a court win.

Writing a nonpayment notice

Two statements belong in the notice. Rent is unpaid, and the landlord intends to terminate the rental agreement unless payment arrives within seven calendar days. Termination rights hinge on written notice of both.

Full payment inside the seven days leaves the landlord with nothing to terminate on. Rent still owed afterward lets the landlord end the agreement and head to court, as described below.

Seven here means calendar days, so weekends and holidays count. Save evidence of the delivery method and date, because the complaint has to show the notice requirements were met.

The 14-day and 30-day lease violation notice

One notice carries both numbers. It describes what the tenant did or failed to do. Termination follows at least 30 days after receipt, unless the tenant corrects the problem within 14 days.

Covered are a failure of the tenant's duties that seriously affects health and safety, and any material breach of the lease. Where repairs, payment of damages or another step can fix it, and the tenant gets that done before the notice date, the lease survives.

  • A return of the same problem inside six months can be ended on written notice of 14 days or more, without a fresh chance to cure.
  • Damages and an injunction are also available to the landlord for noncompliance.
  • Willful noncompliance can bring reasonable attorney's fees.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nebraska house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The five-day notice

The short five-day track is for serious conduct by the tenant, a household member, a guest or anyone the tenant controls: violent crime, illegal sale of a controlled substance, or other acts that endanger other tenants, the landlord or the landlord's staff. Curing is not an option.

The statute gives examples: assault or a threat of it, unlawful use of a firearm or other weapon, a controlled substance the tenant knew or should have known was present, and conduct that threatens or causes property damage. Incidents behind the suit must be spelled out in the complaint.

An innocent tenant has a shield. If an outsider, not the tenant or a household member, is responsible and the tenant seeks a protective order or reports to law enforcement, the landlord cannot rely on this notice. Someone who commits domestic violence is not covered.

Ending a month-to-month tenancy without a reason

Landlord or tenant may end a month-to-month tenancy with a written notice that gives 30 days or more before the rental date it names. For week-to-week the minimum is seven days before the termination date.

Without a stated term, Nebraska treats a lease as monthly, or weekly for a roomer who pays weekly. Inherited a house with an occupant and no written lease? Expect that default to apply.

Staying on after the term or after termination, without consent, exposes a tenant to a possession suit. A willful holdover in bad faith can add up to three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages, whichever is greater, along with reasonable attorney's fees.

What happens in court

Once the notice period ends, the landlord files a complaint for restitution at the district or county court clerk's office. The complaint states the legal basis for possession, the facts, a fairly accurate description of the premises, and the steps taken to meet the notice rules.

  1. A summons and a copy of the complaint go out from the court. Service has to be made within three days and the return is due within five days, with nonjudicial days excluded from both counts.
  2. The judge decides the case alone, with no jury.
  3. A judgment against the tenant forfeits the rental agreement.
  4. If the landlord asks, the court issues a writ of restitution that orders the constable or sheriff to return possession, on a date within ten days of the writ.

Only an officer carrying out a writ can return possession. No notice, by itself, changes who may stay in the house.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nebraska houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Limits on retaliation

Landlords cannot answer a code complaint with a rent increase, lost services, or a possession suit or threat. That covers complaints to a housing or building code agency about a health and safety violation, and joining a tenants' union. A tenant who proves it has a defense to the possession case.

Exceptions let the landlord still sue. These are a violation caused mainly by the tenant's lack of reasonable care, rent that is behind, and compliance that would require work depriving the tenant of the unit. Reasonable rent increases stay allowed.

When a tenant dies, the landlord has ten days to make a reasonable attempt to reach the person the tenant named for retrieving belongings. That person gets 20 days after contact to say the property will be claimed, then 20 more days to take it away.

Eviction and selling the house

You have three options when a tenant lives in the house: finish the notice and court steps and then list, sell around the tenant, or find a buyer who accepts the house as is. The lease, the case's progress and your closing deadline decide which.

  • Save the lease, rent ledger, each notice and delivery proof.
  • Check for an open complaint, judgment or writ, since a buyer will weigh those papers.
  • Deeds recorded July 18, 2026 or later carry the $3.32 per $1,000 documentary stamp tax and need a Form 521.

Cash Home Buyers can purchase a house while an eviction is underway, so you need not wait for a judgment and writ. This page outlines notice rules from Nebraska's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and is not legal advice. Before serving a notice, read the current statutes or consult a Nebraska attorney.

Frequently asked questions

How long is a Nebraska eviction notice for unpaid rent?

Seven calendar days after a written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate. Paying within that time stops the termination.

Can a Nebraska landlord evict without going to court?

No. The landlord must file a complaint for restitution, and only a constable or sheriff holding a writ of restitution can return possession.

How long does a tenant have to leave after a judgment?

The writ's possession date must fall within ten days of its issue. The court issues it after judgment when the landlord asks.

What notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Nebraska?

A written notice given 30 or more days ahead of the rental date it names. Either party may send it, and no reason is needed.

Does the tenant get a chance to fix a lease violation?

Usually, with 14 days to remedy before the agreement ends 30 or more days after receipt. A repeat within six months allows 14 days' notice with no cure, and violent or dangerous conduct allows five days' notice with no cure.
